tldr: We built OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile benchmark with tasks fully aligned between simulation and the real world. Through it, we revealed OpenVTLA, an optimal design recipe for incorporating tactile feedback into pretrained VLA models.
hero_caption: Overview of OpenViTac. It completely pairs simulation and real-world environments across four capability dimensions: property perception, handling fragile objects, contact-rich manipulation, and precision positioning. It enables unified evaluation across multiple tactile sensors and robot hands.
overview:
Advances in vision-language-action (VLA) models have greatly propelled general robot manipulation forward. However, camera images alone cannot fully capture physical states such as object stiffness, friction, and contact forces. This has spurred strong interest in VTLA models that integrate tactile sensing. Unfortunately, existing evaluation frameworks rely on disjoint sensors, robots, and evaluation protocols. They also lack consistency between simulation and the real world, preventing systematic comparisons of how tactile feedback truly helps.

To address this gap, the authors propose OpenViTac, a visuo-tactile benchmark that seamlessly links simulation and reality. They organize contact manipulation into four capability dimensions: Property Perception, Fragility-Aware manipulation, Contact-Rich manipulation, and Precision Manipulation. Matching paired task environments were constructed in Isaac Sim and on a real Franka setup with Robotiq grippers.

Furthermore, the authors explored the design space of how to inject tactile data into a pretrained vision foundation model ($\pi_{0.5}$). They found that a simple approach works best: directly prepending a temporal tactile-specific representation (AnyTouch2) as input tokens to the VLM. They named this framework OpenVTLA.

In experiments across both simulation and the real world, OpenVTLA achieved success rates that significantly outperformed existing VLA, world-action model (WAM), and VTLA baselines. Moreover, sim-and-real co-training—mixing in simulation demonstrations with diversified appearances—substantially improved performance and disturbance robustness, even with a fixed number of real-world demonstrations.
contributions: Organizing contact-oriented manipulation into four capability dimensions and building OpenViTac, a unified visuo-tactile benchmark with paired tasks and assets between simulation and the real world.

Systematically comparing tactile representations (static image vs. temporal) and integration strategies (input concatenation, feature modulation, action conditioning, separate expert, and post-refinement) for pretrained VLAs, and proposing OpenVTLA with the best-performing design.

Demonstrating a strong correlation between simulation and real-world evaluations (Pearson correlation coefficient $r=0.967$), proving that simulation serves as a reliable testbed for tactile policies.
Showing that sim-and-real co-training, which blends diverse simulation data with real-world demonstrations, boosts real-world task success rates and robustness against lighting changes.

sections.heading: Why Do Robots Need a Unified Benchmark for Touch as Well as Vision?
sections.summary: Large vision-language-action models are powerful, but tactile feedback is essential for directly perceiving contact forces and physical properties. Because prior work suffered from mismatched sensors, protocols, and sim-to-real alignment, this paper proposes the unified benchmark OpenViTac.
sections.details:
Recent VLA models (Vision-Language-Action frameworks that directly predict robot actions from visual inputs and instructions) have achieved remarkable progress. However, policies relying solely on vision cannot perceive invisible physical properties such as object stiffness, friction, contact slippage, and subtle contact forces.

This has prompted a shift toward VTLA models that integrate vision, touch, and language. Yet a major obstacle stood in the way: different studies used different tactile sensors (such as GelSight) and varying tasks, making fair comparisons of what actually drives performance gains impossible. Existing manipulation benchmarks (such as LIBERO) are predominantly vision-centric, and benchmarks supporting tactile sensing lacked proper correspondence between simulation and reality.

This is the starting point of this work. The authors categorized diverse contact-rich tasks into four capability dimensions and developed OpenViTac, a benchmark with meticulously paired simulation and real-world setups. They also investigated the optimal way to adapt pretrained VLAs to touch, presenting a new framework called OpenVTLA.

In simulation evaluations, while the strongest VLA, WAM, and existing VTLA achieved average success rates of only 51.5%, 53.3%, and 61.2% respectively, OpenVTLA reached 68.7%. It similarly dominated baselines in real-world experiments, scoring 54.6%.

sections.heading: The Current Landscape of Visuo-Tactile Robot Learning and Benchmarks
sections.summary: While tactile representation learning and contact-aware policy learning are actively studied, systematic comparisons of adaptation strategies have been missing. Sim-and-real aligned tactile benchmarks were also absent, a gap that OpenViTac now fills.
sections.details:
### Trends in Visuo-Tactile Robot Learning
Robot foundation models have developed primarily around VLAs and WAMs (World-Action Models, which combine world model predictions with action generation). Various approaches have emerged to inject touch into these architectures: modulating intermediate features using FiLM, conditioning action generation experts, or adding dedicated tactile experts. However, no prior study systematically compared these strategies on an identical backbone. This paper conducts a cross-cutting comparison using the open $\pi_{0.5}$ model as a common backbone.

### Challenges in Datasets and Benchmarks
Although tactile representation learning datasets have grown, benchmarks for policy evaluation remain in their infancy. Existing simulation environments (such as UniVTAC and NeoSim) lack direct correspondence to real-world tasks, leaving sim-to-real transferability and relative performance ranking unverified. OpenViTac solves this issue by offering environments perfectly paired with real-world assets and task designs.

sections.heading: Benchmark Design Bridging Sim and Real, Plus the OpenVTLA Integration Framework
sections.summary: OpenViTac classifies contact tasks into four capabilities and provides matching simulation environments and data collection pipelines. On this foundation, the authors evaluated tactile representations and integration strategies, establishing OpenVTLA with the most effective setup.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Benchmark Design and Four Capability Dimensions
OpenViTac organizes contact tasks where visual cues alone fall short into four capability dimensions (11 simulation tasks and 8 real-world tasks in total):
- Property Perception (PP): Tasks requiring touch to distinguish physical attributes, such as identifying weight, stiffness, or roughness, and sorting empty cans.
- Fragility-Aware Manipulation (FA): Tasks requiring force control to avoid applying excessive force, such as gently grasping and transporting potato chips without crushing them.
- Contact-Rich Manipulation (CR): Assembly tasks like maintaining gear engagement or stably pulling open a drawer.
- Precision Manipulation (PR): Contact-guided tasks with tight geometric tolerances, such as inserting a USB drive into a port or fitting tight blocks together.

For asset conversion from real to sim, the pipeline reconstructs shapes from multi-view images and decomposes functional parts. It also allows easy generation of appearance-diversified simulation data by varying backgrounds and lighting.

### 3.2 Tactile Adaptation for Pretrained VLAs and OpenVTLA
Training a large VTLA from scratch is difficult due to data constraints, so the authors investigated how to best add touch starting from the pretrained $\pi_{0.5}$ model. They explored two axes:
- Tactile Representation: Whether to use the standard VLA visual encoder (SigLIP) or dedicated tactile encoders (T3, Sparsh, AnyTouch2).
- Tactile Integration: ① Concatenating tokens at the VLM input, ② Feature modulation, ③ Conditioning the action expert directly, ④ Parallel tactile expert, and ⑤ Post-action refinement.

This comparison showed that using AnyTouch2 (which compactly compresses temporal frames) and prepending its tokens directly to the visual tokens at the VLM input (① Token-level concatenation) achieved the best results. Without extra modules, this simple structure lets touch interact with vision and language across all VLM layers. They named this framework OpenVTLA.

### 3.3 Sim-and-Real Co-Training
Taking advantage of OpenViTac's paired setups, the authors designed a sim-and-real co-training scheme that blends fixed real-world demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_r$ with appearance-diversified simulation demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_s$. With coordinate frames and control frequencies synchronized across sim and real, policies are trained jointly using flow matching action cloning loss.

sections.heading: Key Experimental Findings: The Importance of Tactile Temporal Dynamics and Input Concatenation
sections.summary: Large-scale evaluations in simulation and on real robots confirmed that OpenVTLA outperforms existing baselines. For tactile representation, a pretrained temporal encoder proved essential, while direct concatenation at the VLM input was the most effective integration strategy.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The evaluation compared six VLAs ($\pi_{0.5}$, StarVLA, InternVLA-A1.5, etc.), three world-action models (such as FastWAM), the existing VTLA baseline FTP-1, and the proposed OpenVTLA. Using around 100 demonstration episodes per task, success rates were rigorously measured in simulation and on real hardware (Franka Hand, GelSight, etc.).

### 4.2 Main Results and Sim-to-Real Correlation
In simulation, OpenVTLA scored a high average success rate of 68.7%, surpassing VLAs (up to 51.5%) and WAMs (up to 53.3%). On the real robot, OpenVTLA similarly achieved 54.6%, compared to 34.0–43.1% for VLA baselines. Tactile benefits were especially pronounced in Property Perception (PP) and Fragility-Aware (FA) tasks. Furthermore, a very strong Pearson correlation coefficient of $r=0.967$ was confirmed between average sim and real scores, proving that performance rankings in simulation transfer faithfully to the real world.

### 4.3 Understanding Tactile Adaptation Mechanisms
In representation comparisons, AnyTouch2 (68.7% average) clearly outperformed Sparsh (64.7%), SigLIP (59.5%), and T3 (58.1%). Temporal input made a decisive difference in tasks where contact states evolve dynamically, such as can sorting and USB insertion. Ablations showed that removing tactile pretraining dropped performance to 56.5%, and replacing past frames with duplicated current frames (removing temporal dynamics) dropped it to 58.4%.

Across integration strategies, concatenating tokens at the VLM input layer outperformed modulating the action expert or applying post-refinement across all categories. It is crucial to let tactile information share the same attention space with language and vision from the earliest stage.

### 4.4 Sim-and-Real Co-Training and Disturbance Robustness
Adding 500 appearance-diversified simulation demonstrations to 100 real-world demonstrations noticeably boosted success rates in USB insertion and gear assembly (averaging a 15-point increase for OpenVTLA). In robustness tests with severe lighting variations, the vision-only $\pi_{0.5}$ suffered catastrophic performance degradation, whereas tactile-equipped OpenVTLA maintained high success rates. This proves that touch serves as a dependable backup against visual disturbances.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Toward Closing the Tactile Sim-to-Real Gap
sections.summary: OpenViTac opens the door to unified visuo-tactile evaluation and sim-and-real co-training. Refining physical simulation fidelity and expanding to deformable object manipulation and multi-finger hands remain important future directions.
sections.details: OpenViTac provides a standardized platform to fairly compare VLAs, WAMs, and VTLAs across simulation and the real world. In addition, the OpenVTLA recipe—injecting pretrained temporal tactile tokens directly at the VLM input—offers clear guidance for extending future foundation models.\n\nAs a limitation, the authors point out the subtle sensing gap between the tactile simulation (TacEx) and real optical sensor outputs. Future work will pursue stricter sensor and camera calibration, while expanding the benchmark to deformable objects such as cloth and food, long-horizon household tasks beyond tabletop setups, and dexterous multi-finger manipulation.

sections.heading: Appendix: Multi-Sensor Support and Task Observation Visualizations
sections.summary: The benchmark supports three representative optical tactile sensors—GelSight, Xense, and NeoteAI—allowing detailed comparisons of differing sensor outputs and visuo-tactile time-series observations across tasks.
sections.details:
OpenViTac's simulation environment is built on NVIDIA Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab, generating tactile images through contact dynamics simulation based on TacEx. By decoupling visual rendering assets from tactile contact geometries, it achieves both visual realism and accurate physical contact.

The benchmark supports three sensors: GelSight, widely used in research, along with Xense and NeoteAI. Even for the identical USB insertion task, contact patterns, marker displacements, and color palettes vary substantially across sensors; OpenViTac captures all of them through a unified interface in both simulation and the real world.

The collected dataset spans approximately 918,000 frames in simulation and 2.1 million frames on real robots per sensor, representing a valuable resource to support future tactile foundation model research.

captions.F5: Visualizations of the same USB insertion task executed with three tactile sensors: GelSight, Xense, and NeoteAI. Alongside main and wrist camera views, distinctive contact patterns on the left and right fingertips can be observed.

takeaways: Treating tactile information as temporal dynamics rather than static frames drastically improves performance in property perception and precision insertion.
When injecting touch into a pretrained VLA, directly prepending tactile tokens to the VLM input sequence works better than complex feature modulators or separate action experts.
Relative benchmark performance in simulation exhibits an exceptionally strong correlation ($r=0.967$) with real-world rankings, making simulation a practical testbed for tactile policies.
Co-training with appearance-diversified simulation demonstrations enhances task success rates and visual disturbance robustness without requiring additional real-world demonstrations.
limitations: A subtle sim-to-real gap regarding surface texture and elasticity still exists between current tactile physics simulation (TacEx) and real optical tactile sensors.
Evaluation tasks are confined to rigid-body tabletop manipulation, omitting deformable objects like cloth or rubber as well as long-horizon multi-stage tasks.
The gripper setup is restricted to two-finger hands (Franka Hand / Robotiq), leaving evaluation of dexterous multi-finger manipulation for future work.
